2.New York’s attachment statute, N.Y.C.P.L.R. 6201, permits prejudgment attachment when, among other grounds, (1) defendant is a
nondomiciliary residing outside the state or an unlicensed foreign corporation, (2) defendant is within the state but diligent efforts to serve defendant
personally have failed, or (3) defendant’s conduct in connection with the property indicates an intent to defraud creditors or frustrate the enforcement
of a potentially unfavorable judgment. Prejudgment attachment also requires the movant to show a probability of success on the merits. See Silverman
Partners, L.P. v. First Bank, 687 F.Supp.2d 269, 293 (E.D.N.Y. 2010). When the purpose of the attachment is security and not jurisdiction, New York
courts require the movant to show “that something, whether it is a defendant’s financial position or past and present conduct, poses a real risk of the
enforcement of a future judgment.” Bank of China v. NBM L.L.C., 192 F.Supp.2d 183, 188 (S.D.N.Y. 2002) (citation and internal quotation omitted).
The court in Bank of China emphasized that the mere “possibility” that defendants will remove their assets out of the state is “too remote” to justify an
order of attachment. In this case, plaintiff justified the need for the levy by showing that defendants had attempted repeatedly to remove their assets
through such devices as issuing payments on transactions that had not taken place, submitting fake bills of lading, trying to sell real estate that served as
collateral on a bank loan, and by attempting to transfer more than $1 million to the Cayman Islands using a forged hypothecation agreement.
2.PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS AND TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDERS

a.Preliminary Injunctions
A preliminary injunction is a form of provisional remedy that protects a plaintiff from irreparable injury—injury that cannot be
redressed through monetary compensation—while preserving the court’s power to enter meaningful relief after a decision on the merits.
By entering a preliminary injunction, the court seeks to maintain the status quo; as the Second Circuit has put it, without the injunction, it
would be “difficult, and sometimes virtually impossible to ‘unscramble the eggs.’ ” Sonesta Int’l Hotels Corp. v. Wellington Assocs., 483
F.2d 247, 250 (2d Cir. 1973).
